sections.title: Disconnect, be quiet, be in the dark

toc.title: Two things to take with you

blocks.p: You might be here because you're in a dorsal vagal shutdown. Or you might be caring for someone who is, like a family member or a therapy client. Either way, I hope you come away with some new language for these experiences, maybe some empathy for yourself or for others, and that you feel less alone and more normal.

Shutdown might be my most popular topic. It consistently gets the most views, the most comments, the most shares. So I wanted to make something that spoke to the common, day-to-day experiences of shutdown, so people in shutdown could relate to others and feel more normal.

I created a survey and sent it out to my email list of a couple thousand people. I got way more responses than I expected: 75 people in shutdown sharing their experiences. This isn't a peer-reviewed study. It's not something worth publishing in journals, at least not yet. But I got a lot.

The survey covered shutdown experiences, how they impact daily functioning, supports, attempts to make change, and coping. It even included messages from the people who responded to other people in shutdown.

Here I'm focusing on the experiences themselves: sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions. I call this [SSIEC](piece:snb154-ssiec-state-sensation-impulse-emotion-cognition). The Polyvagal state, that's the first S, leads to sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions.
I listed a whole bunch of emotion words in the survey and let people pick as many as they related to.
At the top, with almost 70 percent of respondents relating to them, were alone and unmotivated.

Why would someone in shutdown not feel motivated? Because in shutdown, they lack energy, and motivation requires energy. The way I understand motivation, it requires flight or fight activation, or mobility, plus the safety state. When you're safe and connected, or at least grounded in the present moment, and you have mobility in your system, you can funnel that activation in a certain direction. I call that motivation.

If you're in shutdown and you have no energy, how could you feel motivated? There's no mobility within you. There's no activation. Shutdown is a conservation state. It's conserving resources for coming out of shutdown and using them in fight and in flight. While you're in shutdown, everything is shutting down. All your bodily processes are slowing down. There's literally no energy. So how could someone in shutdown be motivated to meet new goals, get a new job, or do better in school? Of course we want them to be, but while you're in an active shutdown, it's very difficult to do those things.

Why would someone feel alone? Because in shutdown, there's an impulse to reduce stimulation and to be by yourself, and part of reducing stimulation is being alone. If you're not around people who are pressuring you, bugging you, or too positive and social and annoying, you might be a little better off, at least in that moment. So part of shutdown is isolating yourself from others, because it just feels more comfortable.

At the heart of shutdown is disconnection. In shutdown, the body is disconnecting from itself, from the environment, and from other people. So why would someone feel alone? Because they're in this state of disconnection.

Numb was next, at 67 percent. Part of shutdown is dissociation, a disconnection from yourself, from the environment, from others, and that includes from your own emotions. When you disconnect from yourself, it's like you exist from the neck up, maybe just in your head. All the stuff happening beneath that, you're really not aware of. You don't feel much at all. So there's a lot of numbness.
At the lower end were rejection, guilt, abandoned, and shame, which kind of surprised me. Each still had 25 percent of respondents identifying with them, so they're still common, just not as common.

To me, these are very specific aspects of shutdown, likely the result of a specific life context. Someone in shutdown is likely to feel numb or alone, because those are prevalent with shutdown. Shame and guilt are more specific. Grief, for example, comes from the loss of a loved one. It's not always there. It's there when something specific happens that brings up the grief. Guilt might be something you got from your parents, a misplaced guilt they projected onto you. Same with shame. So those aren't with everyone in shutdown, but a specific context might have led to them in a particular person.
What I was surprised by is sad. I associate sadness with shutdown a lot, but apparently not necessarily. Sad was only at 50 percent. That's still a lot, but I expected more.

Depression and sadness often come along with shutdown. But those are both emotions, and someone in shutdown might not feel their emotions. So they may not feel sad. They might not feel depression. They might feel numb, and numb was at 67 percent. More people related to numb than to the specific emotions of sadness and depression.
People also wrote in their own words. Here are a handful:

ul: Wondering what's wrong.
Easily agitated or frustrated.
Despair and exiled.
Misunderstood.
Utterly lonely, afraid to speak up, afraid to make any moves, unloved, unnoticed, unwanted, not needed, not important enough to speak up, to do a single thing.
Powerless.
Thwarted, defeated, and stuck.
Worthless.
Hopeless and longing.
Alien.
I don't give a sh**. Apathy.
Desperation.

blocks.p: Agitation, frustration, and irritation are common when coming out of shutdown into fight, so "easily agitated or frustrated" might be that. Thank you to everyone who responded and shared your own words.
What about thinking in shutdown, the cognitions?

The highest, by far, was disconnected, at over 77 percent. Defense is disconnection: flight, fight, shutdown, freeze. The safety state is connection. If you're not in a safety state, there's some level of disconnection. I would argue shutdown is the most disconnected of all the states. And the more dissociation that comes with shutdown, the more disconnection comes along with it. That could be part of why the experience of thinking is disconnected for someone in shutdown.

There's also this experience in shutdown of watching yourself from above. There are words and thoughts here, but my existence, my thoughts, are floating outside of my body. I've had clients tell me they feel like they're viewing their life through a movie screen. One person was so disconnected from themselves that they weren't even in the audience. They were in the projector box, zoomed out, in this little dark room watching the movie of their life on the screen. That's how disconnected they felt.

Deb Dana put it this way when I interviewed her: "If in sympathetic you're my enemy, in dorsal you don't exist. In dorsal, I'm just floating on my own out there somewhere." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

Disconnected is not a super descriptive word. I wish I'd used something different, but it did have a high response rate. The words in the middle of the survey actually describe disconnected better. They're like flavors of disconnection:

ul: Discouraged, at 57 percent.
Clouded, at 54 percent. Thoughts are muddy or cloudy or foggy, and you're trudging along through them.
Slow, at 49 percent.
Wishing things were different, at 49 percent.
Hopeless, at 47 percent.

blocks.p: All of those sound pretty disconnected, right?

On the lower end was minimizing, at 16 percent. Which I guess is not that big of a deal. That's a joke. Pessimistic was at 28 percent, and negative thinking was at 29 percent, which I was actually pretty surprised at.

I was also surprised minimizing was so low. I thought it would be higher. Maybe minimizing is more of a flight or fight thing. I think minimizing can sound different from different states. In my book Trauma and the Polyvagal Paradigm, I wrote about something called cognitive adaptations: how we take our cognitive skills, like minimizing or catastrophizing, and how those skills can look different in the different states.
People also wrote in their own cognitions:

ul: I'm broken, and a mistake.
Seeking relief but unsure how.
Constantly going over how I ended up in these states and what I could have done differently.
Powerless, fear that time is running out, looping, and can't escape the loop.
Like I'm a failure, unworthy, not meant to be alive, or a mistake in society.
Thinking of my own death, thinking I must deserve bad things.
That I deserve better. How can other people get it done, but I can't?

blocks.p: How about the sensations of shutdown? This is the stuff underneath the emotions. How do you know you have an emotion? When you feel happy, how can you tell? Happiness has a feeling in your body. I call those sensations.
Heavy and disconnected were at the top, with almost 70 percent of respondents relating to them.

Disconnected again. As a sensation, I think it feeds into the emotion of loneliness, and probably into numbness and dissociation too. Disconnection as an underlying sensation of those emotions is pretty prevalent. Disconnection is a big part of shutdown.

Why heavy? Because there's no energy. In shutdown, everything's slowing down. So there's a sense of heaviness, of being pulled down, or of having something draped on top of you. In shutdown, the body kind of wants to collapse. It wants to immobilize. There's no energy to it, and it just feels like it's being pulled down.
In the middle of the sensation words were empty at 54 percent, numb and hollow both at 45 percent, unreal at 37 percent, and invisible at 35 percent.

On the lower end were faint and folded at 10 percent, and floating at around 13 percent. Floating describes dissociation, or some degree of dissociation, where you feel disconnected from your body. Dissociation and floating come from shutdown, but not everyone in shutdown has that experience.

If you're entering into a dissociative, more disconnected, floaty kind of feel, you're getting deeper into shutdown. People can be in shutdown and still function day to day, but the deeper you get into shutdown, the more disconnected and potentially dissociative you become. Floating is one of those words. Same with faint. The extreme of shutdown is actually playing dead and fainting.

I was surprised the sensation of small was only at 25 percent. I thought that would be higher. My clients in more of a shutdown, depressed kind of state often feel pretty damn small, and they report it frequently.
People also described their sensations:

ul: Difficulty feeling my body, even when consciously touching different parts of my body. That's a very disconnected, potentially dissociative kind of state.
I am not here anymore.

Like there's a very heavy blanket on my body that I didn't want. That's on the outside. On the inside, it feels like my blood is not moving, or stagnant. Like I am only a head and torso, and all of my limbs are sleeping or just gone. Like my heart needs warm stimulation before any parts of my body are able to keep up.
I exist in my head, and my head is only doing what's on your thinking list. Beyond the words on the thinking list, there are no sensations.
Like I'm outside of myself.

blocks.p: The last piece is the impulses of shutdown. What does your body want to do from shutdown?

Isolate was alone at the top, with 84 percent of people identifying with it. That's pretty darn high. Why would isolation be at the top? Everything's a threat. You want to be alone. You want lower stimulation, and that means cutting people out and being by yourself. Everything's overwhelming. Even being around people who otherwise might be safe, who otherwise might be co-regulators, might be too much in a deep enough shutdown.

blocks.h3: Disconnect, be quiet, be in the dark

blocks.p: Next were disconnect and be quiet, at 67 and 70 percent. Again, that's isolating with lower stimulation. Disconnection and quiet probably feed into isolating. But you can disconnect and be with someone you care about. You can be in quiet and be with someone you care about. So I don't think you necessarily have to isolate for that.
Be in the dark was at 34 percent. A lot of my shutdown clients want to be alone with lower stimulation, in the dark, maybe with a small light on in the room. So I was surprised it was that low.

At the bottom of the impulses was "I feel like dying," at 22 percent. This is probably more the extreme of shutdown. The body in shutdown is preparing for death. If that's the state of the body, the thoughts follow. Story follows state, according to Deb Dana. So thoughts of death can creep in. That might be outright thoughts of suicide, but it could also be general thoughts like "I wish I wasn't here," or "People would be better off without me," or "It'd be easier if I wasn't alive."

Those kinds of thoughts of death come from shutdown. But even though shutdown is a conservation state that's kind of preparing for death, not everyone is going to be consciously thinking about that. Even while the body is preparing for it, a person might not be deep enough in shutdown for their thoughts to be colored by that state.
People also told me specifically what they want to do:

ul: Sleep, nap, be in bed, lie horizontal, and escape into background noise. Very, very, very common.
Nothing. Zone out, sit still, sleep forever.
Not feel or think, and be in small spaces, for example, wrapped up in bed.
Watch YouTube or movies for hours or days.
I want to mentally and soulfully speak words into the universe and connect me to anyone out there in the world for comfort.
I also want to be contacted by my friends who always support me. It breaks my shutdown in a good way.
To feel supported in my choice to be lonely. To be understood, is what I'm hearing.
To have a cloak of invisibility.

blocks.p: What we want to do from shutdown can be different things. One is what our state truly wants, which might be lower stimulation, being alone, and having quiet, so that we can feel the shutdown: feel grief, or feel alone. But from shutdown, we might also want to do other things just to feel better, like numbing out with YouTube and TikTok or whatever else. Those are things we do to make our feelings go away, and that's different.

Let's combine the answers with the highest response rates and see if we can come up with a general description. Someone in shutdown feels alone and unmotivated. Their thinking is disconnected, discouraged, and clouded. They experience an underlying heaviness and disconnection, and they want to isolate with lower stimulation. I think that's a pretty good picture of shutdown.

Someone in shutdown is generally disconnected, and they generally want to disconnect. On some level, their body has this impulse to disconnect, be alone, and be in lower stimulation. Their daily existence is cut off in every way. Emotionally, they feel alone, and then they cut themselves off from others by isolating. Not everyone, of course, but often. Their thinking is a struggle. It's like they're disconnected from themselves, their cognitions cut off from their body. And their cognitions reinforce their aloneness with thoughts like "It's too hard," or "I can't handle it," or "What's the point?" or "I knew it, I can't do this, I'm worthless." And their impulses are telling them to be alone and to disconnect.

The experience of shutdown is disconnection. And the reason someone is in shutdown is also disconnection. Ongoing, severe shutdown comes from chronic disconnection, from repeatedly being cut off from safe others: in childhood, in an abusive relationship, in captivity. Any sort of prolonged, inescapable potential death can lead to shutdown, and more particularly might lead to fawning or appeasing. I personally argue these come from shutdown. They might be particular flavors of shutdown, but I think they're mostly driven by it. Shutdown can also come from losing a loved one, and through grieving.
So day to day, shutdown is experienced as disconnection, and it comes from disconnection.
If shutdown is disconnection, then what's the solution? The solution to shutdown is reconnection.

I know that's scary if you're in shutdown. It's still the solution. But don't let that scare you, because I don't expect you to go and completely reconnect with yourself, the environment, and people right this moment.

Instead, look for tolerable reconnection: connecting to the environment, to others, and to yourself in tolerable ways. That means slowly reorienting to the environment, slowly coming out of your shell and reconnecting with others, and slowly allowing yourself to feel the full range of who you are. Don't expect to force your way out of shutdown all at once. Let yourself come out of it a little bit at a time.

Use your senses: sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell. Whatever sense you have the most access to, maximize it. Use it. Identify with your senses what helps you feel connection to the external environment.

Not everyone. Not random people, not strangers, and maybe not even people in your life who are obvious red flags or obvious danger cues. Instead, find someone who is a predictable source of safety or comfort for you. If you have it, that could be someone you know personally. It could be a therapist or a coach. It might just be getting a smile here and there when you're out walking your dog. These little, tolerable moments of connection can help someone come out of shutdown little by little.

That means listening to your needs. If what you need is to immobilize and reduce stimulation, that's okay. I don't want you to indulge in it, meaning oversleep, stay in the dark, and watch TikTok all day. That's not listening to your needs. No one needs that. Listening to your need for lower stimulation looks like turning the lights off, or turning on a small dimmer bulb, having quiet, being alone, and just breathing and noticing your breath, listening to the sounds around you, using your senses. If that's what your body needs, listen to it and let it happen.
No, it's not a one-time fix. You have to do this repeatedly, and continually practice allowing shutdown while in safety.

The most important part of reconnecting with yourself is being in your safety state. You're in shutdown. It is what it is. Don't fight it. Instead, prioritize being in your safety state. Identify what brings you to safety, and practice it repeatedly, over and over again.

As you get better at that, you'll be much better at reconnecting with all of you, including sadness and guilt and grief and shame. You'll be able to feel those internal sensations of heaviness and emptiness and numbness, but while anchored in safety.

blocks.h: Two things to take with you

blocks.p: First, I hope you can validate your true experiences instead of ignoring them, minimizing them, or coping them away. Acknowledge them. They are there. They are real. You do feel alone. You do feel sad. You do want to reduce your stimulation. Whatever it is, validate it. Say it out loud if you need to. Write it down. That doesn't mean you indulge in it. It means you acknowledge it. Hopefully you got some new language here to help you do that.

Second, I hope you feel more normal. I hope seeing part of the results of this survey helps you feel like, "Oh, I'm not alone in this state. I'm not alone in these experiences. Other people out there understand what I'm going through, or are going through the same thing." You're not alone in your experiences. There are so many other people out there in shutdown.
